Running &#96;tsc --build&#96; from the root of the workspace ensures that projects are compiled in the correct order based on their dependencies.\n\n\u003e In a more complex setup you might need to rely on additional tooling such as Nx that has a task pipelines functionality built-in.\n\nThe resulting structure of the &#96;dist&#96; folder looks like this: (notice the &#96;*.js&#96; and &#96;*.d.ts&#96; files)\n\n&#96;1ts-monorepo-linking2 ├─ apps3 │ └─ myapp4 │ ├─ ...5 │ ├─ package.json 6 │ └─ tsconfig.json 7 ├─ package.json 8 ├─ packages9 │ └─ lib-a 10 │ ├─ dist11 │ │ ├─ index.d.ts 12 │ │ ├─ index.d.ts.map 13 │ │ ├─ index.js 14 │ │ ├─ index.js.map 15 │ │ └─ tsconfig.tsbuildinfo 16 │ ├─ package.json 17 │ ├─ src 18 │ │ └─ index.ts 19 │ └─ tsconfig.json 20 ├─ tsconfig.base.json 21 └─ tsconfig.json 22&#96;\n\nTo make the compiled &#96;lib-a&#96; usable for other packages, we need to update its &#96;package.json&#96; to point to the compiled artifacts in &#96;dist&#96;. Here's the updated version:\n\npackages/lib-a/package.json\n\n&#96;1{2 \"name\": \"@ts-monorepo-linking/lib-a\",3 \"version\": \"0.0.0\",4 \"private\": true,5 \"type\": \"module\",6 \"exports\": {7 \".\": {8 \"types\": \"./dist/index.d.ts\",9 \"import\": \"./dist/index.js\",10 \"default\": \"./dist/index.js\" 11 },12 \"./package.json\": \"./package.json\" 13 },14 \"main\": \"./dist/index.js\",15 \"types\": \"./dist/index.d.ts\",16 \"module\": \"./dist/index.js\" 17}18&#96;\n\n### Observations: Pre-building Packages\n\n**Dependency resolution:**  \nPrecompiling dependent packages allows the application bundler to rely on prebuilt outputs, avoiding the need to compile package dependencies during application bundling. Each package is now self-contained, with its compiled outputs and defined entry points in the &#96;package.json&#96;. By precompiling and packaging the library, it can be distributed outside the monorepo if needed, which enhances its modularity and reusability. However, the primary focus remains internal use within the monorepo.\n\n**Performance:**  \nThis setup can slightly improve type-checking performance, especially within code editors. Since the type information is already generated as &#96;.d.ts&#96; files during precompilation, the editor can directly rely on these instead of processing TypeScript source files through project references. While cached project references can achieve similar speeds, precompiled declaration files might potentially reduce some overhead.\n\n## Which One Should I Choose?\n\nHere are some thoughts on which approach to use.\n\n**TypeScript Path Aliases: A Simple Option**\n\nTypeScript path aliases have been a reliable way to manage package resolution, particularly before package managers introduced the workspaces feature. They're straightforward to set up, requiring only a global &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; without additional. However, there are limitations to consider as they require additional bundling support/alias resolvers at runtime and might come with some performance degradation in large workspaces.\n\nIsn't Nx using TS Path Aliases?\n\n**Workspaces: The Recommended Approach**\n\nWith widespread support in modern package managers (NPM, PNPM, Yarn, Bun), the workspaces feature has become the preferred method for managing package resolution. It aligns closely with the Node.js platform, leveraging native package resolution mechanisms that also work at runtime. This eliminates the portability issues inherent to TypeScript path aliases.\n\nWhen combined with **TypeScript project references**, this method becomes even more powerful. Workspaces handles package linking such that Node can resolve them properly, while TypeScript project references optimize type-checking and enable incremental builds (for TypeScript). Together, they improve performance, reduce memory usage, and simplify dependency management in larger workspaces. This combination is the recommended way to structure and manage TypeScript packages in a monorepo.\n\n**To Prebuild or Not to Prebuild?**\n\nPrebuilding packages isn't always necessary. Modern bundlers like Vite and Rspack are optimized for speed, often making in-place compilation sufficient. Some things to consider:\n\n* **Cost of Prebuilding:** Precompiling packages introduces a small overhead, as each package must be built individually. Tools like Nx mitigate this cost with computation caching, allowing you to skip redundant builds. If cache results are available, builds can be significantly faster.\n* **Selective Prebuilding:** Prebuilding doesn't have to be applied universally. You can start without prebuilding and add it for specific subsets of your projects, such as the leaf nodes in your monorepo's project graph.\n* **External Publishing:** Prebuilding is essential if your packages need to be published outside the monorepo with tools like Nx release.\n\n## Are There Any Downsides to TypeScript Project References?\n\nWhile TypeScript project references offer significant benefits, they can be maintenance-heavy, especially in large workspaces where their incremental type-checking capabilities are most valuable. The challenge lies in keeping the references array in each &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; file up to date, ensuring all project dependencies are correctly linked.\n\nThis is where Nx comes in, eliminating much of the manual effort involved in maintaining TypeScript project references:\n\n* **Automated Setup with Generators:** Nx provides generators for scaffolding applications and library packages. These generators handle the &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; setup automatically, ensuring that TypeScript project references are correctly configured from the start.\n* **Automatic Synchronization:** Nx includes a sync command that is automatically triggered before critical operations like building or serving a project. This command verifies whether the TypeScript project references are in sync across the workspace. If discrepancies are found, Nx automatically updates the references arrays, keeping your configuration consistent and accurate without manual intervention.\n\n## Wrapping Up\n\nWe've explored various strategies for configuring TypeScript-based packages in a monorepo, starting with relative imports, moving to TS path aliases, and finally leveraging the workspaces in combination with TypeScript project references.\n\nIf you want to try these approaches, check out the companion GitHub repository at \u003chttps://github.com/juristr/ts-monorepo-linking\u003e, or create a new workspace with Nx:\n\n❯\n\nnpx create-nx-workspace mymonorepo --workspaces\n\n\u003e Note &#96;--workspaces&#96; is a temporary flag to instruct Nx to generate a workspaces based monorepo setup.\n\nAlso check out our docs:\n\n* TypeScript Project Linking\n* Switching to Workspaces and Project References\n\n---\n\n## Learn More\n\n* 🧠 Nx Docs\n* 👩‍💻 Nx GitHub\n* 💬 Nx Official Discord Server\n* 📹 Nx Youtube declarations\n* Version Changes\n\nEdit this page on GitHub Scroll to top \n\nAPI ReferenceConfigurationTypeScript\n\nCopy page\n\n# TypeScript\n\nNext.js comes with built-in TypeScript, automatically installing the necessary packages and configuring the proper settings when you create a new project with &#96;create-next-app&#96;.\n\nTo add TypeScript to an existing project, rename a file to &#96;.ts&#96; / &#96;.tsx&#96;. Run &#96;next dev&#96; and &#96;next build&#96; to automatically install the necessary dependencies and add a &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; file with the recommended config options.\n\n\u003e **Good to know**: If you already have a &#96;jsconfig.json&#96; file, copy the &#96;paths&#96; compiler option from the old &#96;jsconfig.json&#96; into the new &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; file, and delete the old &#96;jsconfig.json&#96; file.\n\n## IDE Plugin \n\nNext.js includes a custom TypeScript plugin and type checker, which VSCode and other code editors can use for advanced type-checking and auto-completion.\n\nYou can enable the plugin in VS Code by:\n\n1. Opening the command palette (&#96;Ctrl/⌘&#96; \\+ &#96;Shift&#96; \\+ &#96;P&#96;)\n2. Searching for \"TypeScript: Select TypeScript Version\"\n3. Selecting \"Use Workspace Version\"\n\nTypeScript Command PaletteTypeScript Command Palette\n\nNow, when editing files, the custom plugin will be enabled. When running &#96;next build&#96;, the custom type checker will be used.\n\nThe TypeScript plugin can help with:\n\n* Warning if the invalid values for segment config options are passed.\n* Showing available options and in-context documentation.\n* Ensuring the &#96;'use client'&#96; directive is used correctly.\n* Ensuring client hooks (like &#96;useState&#96;) are only used in Client Components.\n\n\u003e **🎥 Watch:** Learn about the built-in TypeScript plugin → YouTube (3 minutes)\n\n## End-to-End Type Safety \n\nThe Next.js App Router has **enhanced type safety**. This includes:\n\n1. **No serialization of data between fetching function and page**: You can &#96;fetch&#96; directly in components, layouts, and pages on the server. This data _does not_ need to be serialized (converted to a string) to be passed to the client side for consumption in React. Instead, since &#96;app&#96; uses Server Components by default, we can use values like &#96;Date&#96;, &#96;Map&#96;, &#96;Set&#96;, and more without any extra steps. Previously, you needed to manually type the boundary between server and client with Next.js-specific types.\n2. **Streamlined data flow between components**: With the removal of &#96;_app&#96; in favor of root layouts, it is now easier to visualize the data flow between components and pages. Previously, data flowing between individual &#96;pages&#96; and &#96;_app&#96; were difficult to type and could introduce confusing bugs. With colocated data fetching in the App Router, this is no longer an issue.\n\nData Fetching in Next.js now provides as close to end-to-end type safety as possible without being prescriptive about your database or content provider selection.\n\nWe're able to type the response data as you would expect with normal TypeScript. For example:\n\napp/page.tsx\n\nTypeScript\n\nJavaScriptTypeScript\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nasync function getData() {\n  const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/...')\n  // The return value is *not* serialized\n  // You can return Date, Map, Set, etc.\n  return res.json()\n}\n \nexport default async function Page() {\n  const name = await getData()\n \n  return '...'\n}\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nFor _complete_ end-to-end type safety, this also requires your database or content provider to support TypeScript. This could be through using an ORM or type-safe query builder.\n\n## Examples \n\n### Type checking next.config.ts \n\nYou can use TypeScript and import types in your Next.js configuration by using &#96;next.config.ts&#96;.\n\nnext.config.ts\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport type { NextConfig } from 'next'\n \nconst nextConfig: NextConfig = {\n  /* config options here */\n}\n \nexport default nextConfig\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n\u003e **Good to know**: Module resolution in &#96;next.config.ts&#96; is currently limited to &#96;CommonJS&#96;. This may cause incompatibilities with ESM only packages being loaded in &#96;next.config.ts&#96;.\n\nWhen using the &#96;next.config.js&#96; file, you can add some type checking in your IDE using JSDoc as below:\n\nnext.config.js\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// @ts-check\n \n/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */\nconst nextConfig = {\n  /* config options here */\n}\n \nmodule.exports = nextConfig\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### Statically Typed Links \n\nNext.js can statically type links to prevent typos and other errors when using &#96;next/link&#96;, improving type safety when navigating between pages.\n\nTo opt-into this feature, &#96;experimental.typedRoutes&#96; need to be enabled and the project needs to be using TypeScript.\n\nnext.config.ts\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport type { NextConfig } from 'next'\n \nconst nextConfig: NextConfig = {\n  experimental: {\n    typedRoutes: true,\n  },\n}\n \nexport default nextConfig\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nNext.js will generate a link definition in &#96;.next/types&#96; that contains information about all existing routes in your application, which TypeScript can then use to provide feedback in your editor about invalid links.\n\nCurrently, experimental support includes any string literal, including dynamic segments. For non-literal strings, you currently need to manually cast the &#96;href&#96; with &#96;as Route&#96;:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport type { Route } from 'next';\nimport Link from 'next/link'\n \n// No TypeScript errors if href is a valid route\n\u003cLink href=\"/about\" /\u003e\n\u003cLink href=\"/blog/nextjs\" /\u003e\n\u003cLink href={&#96;/blog/${slug}&#96;} /\u003e\n\u003cLink href={('/blog' + slug) as Route} /\u003e\n \n// TypeScript errors if href is not a valid route\n\u003cLink href=\"/aboot\" /\u003e\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTo accept &#96;href&#96; in a custom component wrapping &#96;next/link&#96;, use a generic:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport type { Route } from 'next'\nimport Link from 'next/link'\n \nfunction Card\u003cT extends string\u003e({ href }: { href: Route\u003cT\u003e | URL }) {\n  return (\n    \u003cLink href={href}\u003e\n      \u003cdiv\u003eMy Card\u003c/div\u003e\n    \u003c/Link\u003e\n  )\n}\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n\u003e **How does it work?**\n\u003e \n\u003e When running &#96;next dev&#96; or &#96;next build&#96;, Next.js generates a hidden &#96;.d.ts&#96; file inside &#96;.next&#96; that contains information about all existing routes in your application (all valid routes as the &#96;href&#96; type of &#96;Link&#96;). This &#96;.d.ts&#96; file is included in &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; and the TypeScript compiler will check that &#96;.d.ts&#96; and provide feedback in your editor about invalid links.\n\n### With Async Server Components \n\nTo use an &#96;async&#96; Server Component with TypeScript, ensure you are using TypeScript &#96;5.1.3&#96; or higher and &#96;@types/react&#96; &#96;18.2.8&#96; or higher.\n\nIf you are using an older version of TypeScript, you may see a &#96;'Promise\u003cElement\u003e' is not a valid JSX element&#96; type error. Updating to the latest version of TypeScript and &#96;@types/react&#96; should resolve this issue.\n\n### Incremental type checking \n\nSince &#96;v10.2.1&#96; Next.js supports incremental type checking when enabled in your &#96;tsconfig.json&#96;, this can help speed up type checking in larger applications.\n\n### Disabling TypeScript errors in production \n\nNext.js fails your **production build** (&#96;next build&#96;) when TypeScript errors are present in your project.\n\nIf you'd like Next.js to dangerously produce production code even when your application has errors, you can disable the built-in type checking step.\n\nIf disabled, be sure you are running type checks as part of your build or deploy process, otherwise this can be very dangerous.\n\nOpen &#96;next.config.ts&#96; and enable the &#96;ignoreBuildErrors&#96; option in the &#96;typescript&#96; config:\n\nnext.config.ts\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport type { NextConfig } from 'next'\n \nconst nextConfig: NextConfig = {\n  typescript: {\n    // !! WARN !!\n    // Dangerously allow production builds to successfully complete even if\n    // your project has type errors.\n    // !! WARN !!\n    ignoreBuildErrors: true,\n  },\n}\n \nexport default nextConfig\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n\u003e **Good to know**: You can run &#96;tsc --noEmit&#96; to check for TypeScript errors yourself before building. This is useful for CI/CD pipelines where you'd like to check for TypeScript errors before deploying.\n\n### Custom type declarations \n\nWhen you need to declare custom types, you might be tempted to modify &#96;next-env.d.ts&#96;. However, this file is automatically generated, so any changes you make will be overwritten. Instead, you should create a new file, let's call it &#96;new-types.d.ts&#96;, and reference it in your &#96;tsconfig.json&#96;:\n\ntsconfig.json\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n{\n  \"compilerOptions\": {\n    \"skipLibCheck\": true\n    //...truncated...\n  },\n  \"include\": [\n    \"new-types.d.ts\",\n    \"next-env.d.ts\",\n    \".next/types/**/*.ts\",\n    \"**/*.ts\",\n    \"**/*.tsx\"\n  ],\n  \"exclude\": [\"node_modules\"]\n}\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Version Changes \n\n| Version | Changes                                                                                                                            |\n| ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| v15.0.0 | [next.config.ts](#type-checking-nextconfigts) support added for TypeScript projects.                                               |\n| v13.2.0 | Statically typed links are available in beta.                                                                                      |\n| v12.0.0 | [SWC](/docs/architecture/nextjs-compiler) is now used by default to compile TypeScript and TSX for faster builds.                  |\n| v10.2.1 | [Incremental type checking](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#incremental) support added when enabled in your tsconfig.json. |\n\nPreviouswebVitalsAttributionNextESLint\n\nWas this helpful?\n\nsupported.\n\nSend\n\n---\n\n---\n\n#### Resources\n\nDocsSupport PolicyLearnShowcaseBlogTeamAnalyticsNext.js ConfPreviews\n\n#### More\n\nNext.js CommerceContact SalesCommunityGitHubReleasesTelemetryGovernance\n\n#### About Vercel\n\nNext.js + VercelOpen Source SoftwareGitHubBlueskyX\n\n#### Legal\n\nPrivacy PolicyCookie Preferences\n\n#### Subscribe to our newsletter\n\nStay updated on new releases and features, guides, and case studies.\n\nSubscribe\n\n© 2025 Vercel, Inc.\n\n---\n\n---",

Right-click: Brands.Nx\n\n## Main navigation\n\nDocsBlog\n\nSolutions\n\nResources\n\nAINx CloudNx Enterprise\n\nPress Ctrl  and K to search\n\nGet started now\n\nNx on GitHubGitHub\n\nNxNx\n\nNx on GitHubGitHubOpen navigation menuOpen navigation panel\n\nBlog\n\nZack DeRose\n\nZack DeRoseZack DeRose\n\nJanuary 27, 2025\n\n# Everything You Need to Know About TypeScript Project References\n\nTypeScript Project References Series\n\nThis article is part of the TypeScript Project References series:\n\n* **Everything You Need to Know About TypeScript Project References**\n* Managing TypeScript Packages in Monorepos\n* A new Nx Experience For TypeScript Monorepos and Beyond\n\nConsider the following workspace:\n\n&#96;1.2├─ is-even3│ ├─ index.ts4│ └─ tsconfig.json5├─ is-odd6│ ├─ index.ts7│ └─ tsconfig.json8└─ tsconfig.json9&#96;\n\nAnd here we can see the relevant code:\n\nis-even/index.ts\n\n&#96;1export function isEven(n: number): boolean {2 return n % 2 === 0;3}4&#96;\n\nis-odd/index.ts\n\n&#96;1import { isEven } from 'is-even';2 3export function isOdd(n: number): boolean {4 return !isEven(n);5}6&#96;\n\nIf we try to run our build script on the &#96;is-odd&#96; project, we see that TypeScript is unable to run the &#96;tsc&#96; command because at the TypeScript level, &#96;is-odd&#96; is not aware of the &#96;is-even&#96; module:\n\nTypescript cannot find the 'is-even' module.\n\n\\~/is-odd❯\n\ntsc\n\n&#96;1index.ts:1:24 - error TS2792: Cannot find module 'is-even'. Did you mean to 2set the 'moduleResolution' option to 'nodenext', or to add aliases to the3'paths' option?4 51 import { isEven } from 'is-even';6 ~~~~~~~~~7 8 9Found 1 error in index.ts:110 11&#96;\n\nTypeScript needs to be informed as to how to find the module named &#96;is-even&#96;. The error message here actually suggests that we may have forgotten to add aliases to the &#96;paths&#96; option. To do this we can adjust our &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; file at the root of the monorepo:\n\ntsconfig.json\n\n&#96;1{2 \"compilerOptions\": {3 \"paths\": {4 \"is-even\": [\"./is-even/index.ts\"],5 \"is-odd\": [\"./is-odd/index.ts\"]6 }7 }8}9&#96;\n\nBy having the individual &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; files &#96;extend&#96; this base config, they will all get these paths, and now our build command will work.\n\nSuccessfully building 'is-odd' package\n\n\\~/is-odd❯\n\ntsc\n\n&#96;1 2&#96;\n\nThe biggest downsides with this approach is that it does not enforce any boundaries within your monorepo. **At the TypeScript level we treat the entire monorepo as one \"unit\"**. The TypeScript path aliases we defined, while seeming to create boundaries, are really just a nicer alternative for relative imports.\n\nTo solve this, TypeScript introduced Project References. Let's have a look.\n\n## TypeScript Project References\n\nBy adding boundaries at the TypeScript level, we can significantly cut down on the \"surface area\" that TypeScript has to contend with when doing its job. This way, rather than TypeScript seeing our entire monorepo as one unit, it can now understand our workspace as a series of connected \"islands\" or nodes.\n\nIslands of TypeScript\n\nTo add this to our previous example, we'll adjust the &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; file for &#96;is-odd&#96; since it depends on &#96;is-even&#96; (note that the &#96;references&#96; field is the only difference from the &#96;is-even/tsconfig.json&#96; file):\n\nis-odd/tsconfig.json\n\n&#96;1{2 \"extends\": \"../tsconfig.json\",3 \"compilerOptions\": {4 \"target\": \"esnext\",5 \"module\": \"esnext\",6 \"forceConsistentCasingInFileNames\": true,7 \"strict\": true,8 \"skipLibCheck\": true 9 },10 \"references\": [{ \"path\": \"../is-even\" }]11}12&#96;\n\nNote that we still actually need path aliases for our example. This is because we still need a mechanism to resolve the location in the import statement:\n\n&#96;1import { isEven } from 'is-even';2&#96;\n\nThere are alternatives to path aliases to allow for this name to be resolved. The most recent enhancements in Nx use the &#96;workspaces&#96; functionality of your package manager of choice (npm/pnpm/yarn/bun) as the way of resolving these names. With a few more adjustments to this set up, we can now use the &#96;-b&#96; or &#96;--build&#96; option when building &#96;is-odd&#96;. One of these is turning on the composite compiler option for each project, which we can do by setting the &#96;compilerOption&#96; of &#96;composite&#96; to &#96;true&#96; at the root &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; file - since our other &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; files for the 2 different projects already extend our root file:\n\ntsconfig.json\n\n&#96;1{2 \"compilerOptions\": {3 \"paths\": {4 \"is-even\": [\"./is-even/index.ts\"],5 \"is-odd\": [\"./is-odd/index.ts\"]6 },7 \"composite\": true 8 }9}10&#96;\n\nLet's run our build now with the &#96;--verbose&#96; flag on:\n\nSuccessful build with Typescript's 'Build Mode'\n\n\\~❯\n\ntsc -b is-odd --verbose\n\n&#96;1Projects in this build:2 * is-even/tsconfig.json3 * is-odd/tsconfig.json4 5Project 'is-even/tsconfig.json' is out of date because buildinfo file 6'is-even/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo' indicates that file 'is-odd/index.ts' was root7file of compilation but not any more.8 9Building project10'/Users/zackderose/monorepo-project-references/is-even/tsconfig.json'...11 12Project 'is-odd/tsconfig.json' is out of date because buildinfo file 13'is-odd/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo' indicates that program needs to report errors.14 15Building project16'/Users/zackderose/monorepo-project-references/is-odd/tsconfig.json'...17&#96;\n\nNotice our filesystem now:\n\n&#96;1.2├─ is-even3│ ├─ index.d.ts4│ ├─ index.js5│ ├─ index.ts6│ ├─ tsconfig.json7│ └─ tsconfig.tsbuildinfo8├─ is-odd9│ ├─ index.d.ts10│ ├─ index.js11│ ├─ index.ts12│ ├─ tsconfig.json13│ └─ tsconfig.tsbuildinfo14└─ tsconfig.json15&#96;\n\nNotice how both &#96;is-even&#96; AND &#96;is-odd&#96; now have a compiled &#96;index.d.ts&#96; declaration file and &#96;index.js&#96;. They also both have a &#96;tsconfig.tsbuildinfo&#96; file now (this holds the additional data TypeScript needs to determine which builds are needed). With the &#96;--build&#96; option, TypeScript is now operating as a build orchestrator - by finding all referenced projects, determining if they are out-of-date, and then building them in the correct order.\n\n## Why This Matters\n\nAs a practical/pragmatic developer - the TLDR of all of this information is project references allow for more performant builds.\n\nWe've put together a repo to demonstrate the performance gains, summarized by this graphic:\n\nresults of the perf measurements for TypeScript project references\n\nIn addition to the time savings we saw reduced memory usage (\\~\u003c 1GB vs 3 GB). This makes sense given what we saw about how project references work. This is actually a very good thing for CI pipelines, as exceeding memory usage is a common issue we see with our clients for their TypeScript builds. Less memory usage means we can use smaller machines, which saves on the CI costs.\n\n## Can I use Project References in Nx?\n\nYes. You benefit from the performance gains of TypeScript project references the most in large monorepos. However, this is also when the biggest downsides of project references are felt, namely having to manually manage all the references in various &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; files. This is what we help automate in Nx.\n\nWe're going to **dive deeper into the new Nx experience with project references in one of the next articles** of the series, but TL;DR, you can experiment with the setup now by either using the &#96;--preset=ts&#96;:\n\n❯\n\nnpx create-nx-workspace@latest foo --preset=ts\n\nOr alternatively by appending the &#96;--workspaces&#96; flag to other presets:\n\n❯\n\nnpx create-nx-workspace@latest reactmono --preset=react --workspaces\n\n\u003e Note, Angular doesn't work with TypeScript project references yet but we're looking into various options to make it happen.\n\n## Next up\n\nStay tuned for our next article in the series about managing TypeScript packages in monorepos.\n\n---\n\n* Nx Docs\n* X/Twitter\n* LinkedIn\n* Bluesky\n* Nx       "chunk": "Skip to main content\n\nKieran Roberts header picture\n\n\\[email protected\\]\n\nBlog | LinkedIn | GitHub | Bluesky \n\n Back to posts\n\nShare:  LinkedIn\n\n Scroll to top\n\nBlog Post Cover Image\n\n# How to setup path aliases for development with Next.js \u0026 Jest\n\nKieran Roberts header picture\n\nApril 16, 2021\n\nUpdated: February 23, 2025\n\n## TLDR: Update (2025)\n\n### Next.js\n\nConfigure the &#96;baseUrl&#96; in the &#96;tsconfig/jsconfig&#96; along with your desired paths:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// tsconfig/jsconfig.json\n{\n  \"compilerOptions\": {\n    \"@/*\": [\"./src/*\"]\n  }\n}\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### Jest\n\nInstall &#96;jest&#96; and &#96;jest-environment-jsdom&#96;:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\npnpm install -D jest jest-environment-jsdom\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nGenerate a Jest configuration:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\npnpm create jest@latest\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nUpdate the jest config file to use &#96;next/jest&#96;:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport type { Config } from 'jest';\nimport nextJest from 'next/jest.js';\n\nconst createJestConfig = nextJest({\n\tdir: './',\n});\n\nconst config: Config = {\n\tcoverageProvider: 'v8',\n\ttestEnvironment: 'jsdom',\n};\n\nexport default createJestConfig(config);\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nFinally match the paths option from your &#96;tsconfig/jsconfig&#96; to the Jest &#96;moduleNameMapper&#96;:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport type { Config } from 'jest';\nimport nextJest from 'next/jest.js';\n\nconst createJestConfig = nextJest({\n\tdir: './',\n});\n\nconst config: Config = {\n\tcoverageProvider: 'v8',\n\ttestEnvironment: 'jsdom',\n\tmoduleNameMapper: {\n\t\t// Your desired paths\n\t\t'^@/src(.*)$': '\u003crootDir\u003e/src/$1',\n\t},\n};\n\nexport default createJestConfig(config);\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYou can find the original article below for reference.\n\n---\n\n## Original article\n\nI wanted to share how you can setup path aliases for your imports. Sometimes you end up with various levels of file nesting and this can get messy fast.\n\nFortunately for us both Next.js and Jest support adding path aliases so we don’t end up with something like this:\n\n&#96;import Component from \"../../../Component/Component\";&#96;\n\nFor any medium to large react project you will have realized that due to the component nature of the library we end up doing a lot of importing. Let’s find out how we can change the above into this:\n\n&#96;import Component from \"@/Component/Component\";&#96;\n\nfor both development in Next.js and for our tests using the test Framework Jest.\n\n## Next.js\n\n### Step 1 - Create a Next app\n\nI’ll start with a brand new project so you can see all the steps. For this I will create a new Next application using &#96;npx create-next-app@latest&#96; so we can get up and running quickly.\n\n### Step 2 - Create some files to import\n\nNext I’m going to create a &#96;src&#96; folder which is where I normally store the apps components, hooks etc. Let’s add some files to our &#96;src&#96; folder to simulate how a real project might look 👇 .\n\nHere I have created the following files\n\n* &#96;Header.js&#96; and &#96;Button.js&#96; components inside a &#96;components&#96; folder\n* &#96;__tests__&#96; folder with our component test files\n* &#96;useStorage.js&#96; hook inside a &#96;hooks&#96; folder\n* &#96;config.js&#96; inside a &#96;lib&#96; folder\n\nThe contents of the files is not important. As long as you export something from your components which I will show you in a second.\n\n### Step 3 - Specify our path aliases\n\nFirst we need to create a &#96;jsconfig.json&#96; file (or &#96;tsconfig.json&#96; if you’re using TypeScript) and setup our path aliases. My setup looks like this 👇.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n{\n  \"compilerOptions\": {\n    \"baseUrl\": \".\",\n    \"@/components\": [\"src/components/*\"],\n    \"@/hooks\": [\"src/hooks/*\"],\n    \"@/lib\": [\"src/lib/*\"]\n  }\n}\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nHere we can specify a base url that we start our import from. Commonly you will see the root &#96;.&#96; specified.\n\nNext we can specify path aliases for our paths to the different folder locations. &#96;paths&#96; is an object where we start with our path alias and assign it an array of paths. A common syntax of alias is in the format &#96;\"@/fileName/\"&#96; but you can use anything you’d like.\n\nLet’s take our &#96;components&#96; alias as an example. We are saying we want to match the alias &#96;\"@/components/\"&#96; to the path &#96;src/components/&#96; folder.\n\n### Step 4 - Checking that our aliases work\n\nNow let’s add some basic code to our components:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Button.js\nexport default function Button() {\n  return \u003cbutton\u003eClick me\u003c/button\u003e\n}\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nand the header is the same except it exports a &#96;\u003ch2 /\u003e&#96; tag 🙂. We can import them into other pages/components using the path aliases like this 👇.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/pages/index.js\nimport Button from '@/components/Button';\nimport Header from '@/components/Header';\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThat’s it! We have successfully setup path aliases for our imports in Next.js.\n\n## Jest\n\n### Step 1 - Install and configure the necessary files\n\nI wanted to add this extra step for two reasons\n\n1. You should be testing your apps\n2. It’s good to keep your imports consistent across development code and tests\n\nFirst let’s download the packages we need to work with Jest. I will install the following packages:\n\n* &#96;jest&#96;\n* &#96;babel-jest&#96;\n\n&#96;jest&#96; if the primary package we need to install in order to use the Jest testing framework. While &#96;babel-jest&#96;will help transform our code so we can include things like ES modules &#96;import&#96; syntax in our test files.\n\nWe also have to configure a &#96;.babelrc&#96; file with the following setup:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n{\n  \"presets\": [\"next/babel\"]\n}\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWhat we are doing here is telling babel to use the custom preset for Next.js.\n\n## Step 2 - Add our &#96;jest.config.js&#96;\n\nFinally we can now get on to our aliases in Jest. We first need to create a &#96;jest.config.js&#96; file. There are a couple of options we will pass in here and it looks something like this.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nmodule.exports = {\n\ttestPathIgnorePatterns: ['\u003crootDir\u003e/node_modules/', '\u003crootDir\u003e/.next/'],\n\tmoduleNameMapper: {\n\t\t'^@/components(.*)$': '\u003crootDir\u003e/src/components/$1',\n\t\t'^@/hooks(.*)$': '\u003crootDir\u003e/src/hooks/$1',\n\t\t'^@/lib(.*)$': '\u003crootDir\u003e/src/lib/$1',\n\t},\n\ttransform: {\n\t\t'^.+\\\\.(js|jsx|ts|tsx)$': '\u003crootDir\u003e/node_modules/babel-jest',\n\t},\n};\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe first thing we do is use the &#96;testPathIgonrePattern&#96; which is defined as an array of strings that specify which paths we would like to skip when testing. Here we include the &#96;node_modules&#96; directory and the &#96;.next&#96; directory which contains our build files.\n\nWe don’t want Jest looking in these directories for tests and we specify these paths starting at the root &#96;\u003crootDir\u003e&#96;.\n\nNext comes our path aliases. We need to use the &#96;moduleNameMapper&#96; property to map our aliases. It is a map of regular expressions and in this case we setup our three current aliases of &#96;@/components&#96; &#96;@/hooks&#96; and &#96;@/lib&#96;.\n\nYou can do this for any path you are likely to be importing regularly. If you wanted to move on to integration tests and import you pages into tests you could do the same for example &#96;@/page&#96;.\n\nThe order in which you setup these aliases could matter however. These patterns are checked by Jest from top to bottom therefore you have more specific rules you should include them first.\n\nFor more information check out the Jest - Configuring Jest.\n\nNow if we add an empty test block to one of our files and attempt the import with the alias we won’t receive any errors after running out test script. Our imports are now working as expected in Jest ✔.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/__tests__/Button.test.js\nimport Button from '@/components/Button';\n\ndescribe('Button', () =\u003e {\n\tit('should do something', () =\u003e {});\n});\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Conclusion\n\nSet up path aliases for cleaner imports in Next.js and Jest by configuring the &#96;baseUrl&#96; and &#96;paths&#96; in your &#96;tsconfig/jsconfig.json&#96;. For Jest, install necessary packages, configure Babel, and set up a &#96;jest.config.js&#96; file with &#96;moduleNameMapper&#96; to map aliases for consistent imports across development and tests.\n\nShare:  LinkedIn\n\n## More posts you might like\n\nBlog Post Cover Image5 Simple Tips/Good Practises to Level Up Your React CodebaseJanuary 23, 20255 simple React tips and good practises: improve maintainability, reusability, performance, and project management effectively.Read more \n\nBlog Post Cover ImageTutorial: Implement a Scroll-Translated, Dynamic Sticky Navbar in ReactJanuary 2, 2025Learn to implement a dynamic, sticky, scroll-aware navbar in React with smooth transitions and accessibility optimization for reduced-motion preferencesRead more \n\n## Table of contents\n\n* TLDR: Update (2025)  \n   * Next.js  \n   * Jest\n* Original article\n* Next.js  \n   * Step 1 - Create a Next app  \n   * Step 2 - Create some files to import  \n   * Step 3 - Specify our path aliases  \n   * Step 4 - Checking that our aliases work\n* Jest  \n   * Step 1 - Install and configure the necessary files\n* Step 2 - Add our jest.config.js\n* Conclusion\n\nkieranroberts.dev\n\nDesign \u0026 build by Kieran.\n\nBlog | LinkedIn | GitHub | Bluesky \n\n© 2025 Kieran Roberts. &#96;app&#96; Router folder or &#96;pages&#96; Router folder to &#96;src/app&#96; or &#96;src/pages&#96; respectively.\n\nAn example folder structure with the &#96;src&#96; folderAn example folder
